title: Open globe and orbital trauma
subtitle: Shield the globe; release a tense orbit with a lateral canthotomy

sources.title: A standardized classification of ocular trauma (Kuhn et al.)
Orbital compartment syndrome: the ophthalmic surgical emergency (Lima et al.)

red_flags.text: An irregular or peaked pupil, a shallow or flat anterior chamber, uveal tissue at the wound, or a deflated globe: open globe injury.
Hammering metal on metal, grinding, or a high-velocity projectile: an intraocular foreign body until a CT says otherwise, even with a tiny entry wound.

After trauma, or after sinus, orbital or lid surgery: proptosis, a tense orbit, reduced vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and restricted eye movements. This is orbital compartment syndrome.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage extending all the way round the cornea with reduced vision: possible occult posterior rupture.
Restricted upgaze with nausea, bradycardia and a white-looking eye in a child after blunt trauma: trapdoor orbital floor fracture with muscle entrapment.

do_now.text: Suspected open globe: apply a rigid shield that rests on the bony orbit, with no pressure on the eye and no pad underneath. Nothing goes into the eye: no drops, no ointment, no tonometry.
Suspected open globe: antiemetic and analgesia to prevent vomiting and straining, nil by mouth, head up. Do not remove a protruding foreign body.
Orbital compartment syndrome with threatened vision: perform lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis at once, without waiting for imaging or an ophthalmologist to arrive.
Check tetanus status and start intravenous antibiotics for an open globe per local protocol, to reduce the risk of endophthalmitis.

assess.text: Visual acuity in each eye, even if only perception of light. It is the strongest predictor of outcome and the baseline for every later decision.
Pupils for a relative afferent pupillary defect, looking only, without pressing on the eye.

Classify the injury: open globe (laceration, penetrating, perforating, intraocular foreign body, rupture) or closed globe (contusion, lamellar laceration). The classification guides prognosis and planning.

Orbital compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: proptosis, a tight orbit that resists gentle retropulsion, raised intraocular pressure, reduced vision or a relative afferent pupillary defect, and ophthalmoplegia. Retropulsion is only tested once an open globe has been excluded.
Examine for associated injuries: head injury, facial fractures, and the cervical spine. Record the GCS alongside the eye findings.

investigate.text: CT of the orbits with fine cuts for suspected open globe, intraocular foreign body, or orbital fracture. Do not request MRI when a metallic foreign body is possible.
Imaging must never delay a canthotomy for a clinical orbital compartment syndrome.
Pre-operative bloods and fasting status for an open globe that will go to theatre.

resuscitate.text: Treat life-threatening injuries first in multiple trauma. The eye waits, shielded, but is not forgotten at handover.
Avoid any pressure on the eye during airway management, transfer and examination. Instruct the team and the patient.

definitive.text: Urgent primary repair of an open globe by ophthalmology, as soon as safely possible, with removal of any intraocular foreign body.

Lateral canthotomy: after local anaesthetic, crush the lateral canthus with a straight haemostat, then cut it horizontally to the orbital rim. Then cantholysis: identify and cut the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon until the lower lid is freely mobile.
After canthotomy, recheck vision, pupil and orbital tension. If the orbit is still tight, add superior cantholysis, and arrange urgent ophthalmology and imaging for the cause.
Orbital floor fractures without entrapment are usually managed with observation and later review; a trapdoor fracture with muscle entrapment in a child needs urgent surgical release.

escalate.text: On-call ophthalmology immediately for every suspected open globe and every orbital compartment syndrome, including after the canthotomy has been done.
Maxillofacial surgery or ENT for orbital fractures, and neurosurgery for associated intracranial injury.
Transfer for open globe repair with the shield in place, nil by mouth, with antiemetic cover and the CT images sent ahead.

notes: A lateral canthotomy is a simple procedure that saves sight. The error is not doing it badly; it is waiting for someone else to do it.
Never check the pressure in an eye that might be open. The shield is the treatment until theatre.
Retrobulbar haemorrhage after sinus or lid surgery presents to the ward or recovery team, not to the eye department. Everyone who looks after these patients should know the signs.
